title: Tang and Song China: The Medieval Superpower

cards.h: China had the world's best inventions 500 years before Europe caught up
cards.b:
Imagine a world city of one million people in 750 CE, with poets, parties and foreign merchants. That was Chang'an, capital of the Tang.

A few centuries later, China's Song era produced printing, paper money and gunpowder weapons. Let us meet them.

After a short Sui dynasty, Li Yuan founded the Tang in 618. His son Li Shimin (Emperor Taizong) was a strong ruler. The empire's capital Chang'an drew traders from Persia, Central Asia and Japan.

Tang poets Li Bai and Du Fu are still loved. Wu Zetian ruled as China's only female emperor (690-705).
In 755 General An Lushan rebelled. The war lasted until 763 and killed millions or left them uncounted; Tang rule never fully recovered. Provincial governors grew stronger. The dynasty ended in 907.
The Song (960-1279) had a booming economy: iron output, cities, banknotes, and ships with compasses. The oldest dated printed book is the Diamond Sutra of 868, found at Dunhuang.

The Song relied heavily on civil service exams. Aspiring officials studied Confucian classics. It was a rare chance, though most successful candidates came from well-off families.

Capital Kaifeng was crowded, with night markets. The Song fell back to the south after the Jurchen took the north in 1127. The Southern Song lasted till the Mongols in 1279.

Foot-binding began in the Song era among elites, and later spread. It hurt women for centuries. The Song also saw the rise of Neo-Confucianism, which put more rules on women's lives.

Progress had a hard side.

cards.h: Did the Chinese invent gunpowder for fireworks?
cards.b:
Myth: it was a toy.Fact: it was found by alchemists looking for medicines, probably in the Tang era. Early Song texts such as the Wujing Zongyao (1044) list recipes for military use, and the Song used bombs and fire-arrows.

Historians also argue about a Song 'industrial revolution' (Mark Elvin's 'medieval economic revolution'). It did not lead to machines like Britain's later one.

Pilgrims and ships

In 629 CE the monk Xuanzang slipped out of Tang China and walked to India. He studied at Nalanda, met Harsha at Kannauj in 643, and came home in 645 with 657 Buddhist texts. His travel record is a key source for Harsha's India.

Around 671 Yijing went by sea, through Srivijaya, and spent about ten years at Nalanda and Tamralipti.

Under the Song, the ships went the other way. The Chola king Rajaraja I sent an embassy to China in 1015, and another followed in 1033. Chinese ships called at Tamil ports as the sea trade boomed.

Five things to remember

  1. The Tang (618-907) had a cosmopolitan capital, Chang'an.
  2. The An Lushan rebellion (755-763) weakened the Tang.
  3. The Song (960-1279) saw printing, paper money, gunpowder and the compass in use.
  4. Civil service exams selected officials.
  5. India and China exchanged monks, envoys and trade.

Think about it

  • Why might invention not always lead to an industrial revolution?
  • What does Chang'an tell you about being open to the world?
